sections.html:
For most owners the cutoff is May 15 or 30 days after the appraisal district's notice, whichever comes later. The 30 days run from the date the district mails the notice, not the day it reaches you.

The district must send a notice of appraised value by May 1 (April 1 for a residence homestead), or soon after, whenever the value is higher than last year. The notice explains how to file and mentions the informal conference option. Open it the day it arrives and write down the mailing date.

File Form 50-132, Property Owner's Notice of Protest, with the appraisal review board (ARB). The form is optional, though. A written notice that names the property, the owner and some disagreement with a district decision is enough.

  • Use Form 50-162 if you want an agent to represent you at the hearing.
  • Lessees who must reimburse the owner's taxes may protest if the owner does not.
  • Off-shore workers and full-time military members may be entitled to file late.

Keep a copy and proof of the filing date, since the deadline controls whether you get a hearing.

The appraised value is the usual subject, but you can contest any district action touching your property. Hearing topics include value, exemptions, special appraisal qualification and the circuit breaker limitation.

Many owners ask whether the tax bill itself can be protested. It cannot. Neither the ARB nor the appraisal district sets your taxes, and the ARB cannot consider your personal finances. Its job is to certify value as the market dictates.

sections.h2: Where the protest fits in the tax year
sections.html:
Protest season sits between the spring notices and the summer roll. The ARB starts hearing protests around May 15 and approves the appraisal records by July 20. By July 25 the chief appraiser certifies the roll to each taxing unit. If more than 5 percent of total appraised value is still under protest, the ARB may hold off on approval.

Units then adopt rates by about the end of September, and bills go out October 1. A successful protest lowers the value those rates are applied to. It leaves the rate alone.

  • Spring: value notice arrives and the protest window opens.
  • Late spring and summer: informal conferences and ARB hearings.
  • July: records approved and roll certified.
  • October: bills mailed, with the tax due by the following January 31.

You can ask the appraisal district for an informal conference, and many protests end right there. If yours does not, it moves on to a formal hearing.

The ARB must give at least 15 days' notice of the hearing date, time, place and subject. At least 14 days before, the district must send the Taxpayer Assistance Pamphlet, the ARB procedures it adopted and a statement that you may request copies of the evidence it plans to use. You may appear in person, by phone or videoconference, or file a written affidavit. In counties above 120,000 people, give an email address or number and you will get electronic notices and reminders.

sections.h2: Evidence that helps at a hearing
sections.html:
Bring proof of value. Saying the district is wrong will not carry the day.

  • Photographs of your property and comparable ones.
  • Repair receipts or estimates.
  • Sales price records, such as listings or closing statements.
  • Median level of appraisal calculations, for an equal and uniform protest.
  • Affidavits, engineering reports, surveys and deed records.

You decide whether to present before or after the district's representative. Each side may present evidence, question witnesses and offer an opinion of value. Stick to facts about value. The ruling covers only the tax year at issue.

A late protest can still get a hearing if you show good cause before the ARB approves the appraisal records. After approval, or without good cause, the right to protest can end.

A few narrower late routes exist, and each requires that the tax not be delinquent.

  • You never received a notice the district was required to send.
  • A motion for correction when a residence homestead was valued at least one-fourth too high.
  • A motion for correction when other property was valued at least one-third too high.
  • A clerical error, duplicate appraisal or ownership error, which can reach back through the current year and five earlier years.
  • A joint motion with the chief appraiser, which the ARB approves if both agree.

This narrow tool targets process problems. After you file a protest, if you believe the ARB or the chief appraiser skipped a procedural requirement, you can ask the Comptroller's office for limited binding arbitration to compel compliance. It does not reopen the value itself.

If you simply disagree with the value, stay with the hearing and the appeal routes in the table below.

An owner or lessee may name a representative on Form 50-162, Appointment of Agent for Property Tax Matters. An agent can attend, present evidence and question the district's witness for you.

The hearing is not the place to argue about the size of your bill or your income. The ARB may weigh general economic and environmental influences on value but not an owner's personal finances. The Comptroller's office cannot advise on a matter under protest, so direct questions about a live case to the appraisal district or the ARB.

After the hearing the ARB sends a written order by email or certified mail. Keep it, because every appeal deadline runs from the day you receive it.

Three routes are open, and the written order comes by email or certified mail.

Appeal options after an ARB order
OptionDeadline from the orderNotes
State district courtPetition within 60 days of receiving the orderCounty where the property sits; consult an attorney first
Regular binding arbitrationRequest to the Comptroller within 60 days of noticeHomestead at any value, or property of $5 million or less; deposit required
State Office of Administrative HearingsNotice to chief appraiser within 30 days; $1,500 deposit within 90 daysARB value over $1 million; value or unequal appraisal only; not industrial property

Whichever you choose, pay at least the undisputed tax before the delinquency date. After a hearing, a court may excuse prepayment if you file an oath of inability to pay.

sections.h2: Protesting when you plan to sell
sections.html:
It can pay off. Appraised value drives the tax bill that gets prorated at closing, so a lower value for the year lowers the amount owed. When the ARB rules in your favor, the chief appraiser notifies the taxing units, and the units send any refund if the taxes were already paid.

Tell your closing agent about a pending protest. If the hearing is still ahead when you close, ask how the title company will handle the proration, since the final value may not be known yet. A buyer paying cash may be more flexible on timing than one waiting on a lender, but the protest itself belongs to the owner of record, so keep the paperwork and the filing proof where you can find them.

Special ARB panels hear commercial, utility, industrial and multifamily property above a value threshold. Single-family owners will not reach it.

faqs.q: When is the Texas protest deadline?
faqs.a: May 15 or 30 days after the appraisal district's notice, whichever is later. The 30 days run from the mailing date.

faqs.q: Do I need a lawyer to protest in Texas?
faqs.a: No. You can file a simple written notice and appear yourself, and Form 50-162 lets you name an agent if you prefer. Talk to an attorney before filing a district court petition.

faqs.q: Can I protest my tax rate?
faqs.a: No. The ARB hears value and related district actions, and it does not set rates. Taxing units adopt rates after notice and hearing.

faqs.q: What if I miss the protest date?
faqs.a: Ask the ARB for a late hearing and show good cause before it approves the appraisal records. Some narrower correction motions also exist, as long as taxes are not delinquent.

faqs.q: How long do I have to appeal an ARB order?
faqs.a: Within 60 days of receiving the order for district court or regular binding arbitration, and within 30 days for the SOAH notice if the ARB value is over $1 million.
